c: Summit Insurance Agency, an office of 30 employees
j: an employee, Maria, whose laptop will not connect to the internet
s: Maria is an insurance agent with a client call in 30 minutes. Her laptop suddenly cannot connect to the office Wi-Fi or open the company's customer database, and she is frustrated. Other coworkers appear to be working normally. You are the service desk technician receiving her call.

Your job is to talk with Maria, gather the facts, troubleshoot step by step, and either fix the problem or escalate it. You can walk her through basic checks, offer a temporary workaround such as a loaner laptop or a phone hotspot, and escalate to the network administrator if needed. The company's policy is to log every ticket.
The judge will play Maria. You have 7 minutes to resolve the issue, keep her informed, and close the ticket.
f: Symptom: laptop cannot connect to Wi-Fi or the customer database; started after a software update this morning
Other employees are not affected
Maria's client call is in 30 minutes
Available workarounds: phone hotspot (internet only), loaner laptop (about 15 minutes to prepare), escalation to the network administrator (response within an hour)
Ticket policy: record the issue, steps taken and resolution
m: a phone call to the service desk
d: help the employee and resolve the ticket
n: Greets Maria, shows empathy and confirms contact information
Asks clear questions about what changed and what she sees
Walks through logical steps: Wi-Fi toggle, airplane mode, network adapter, restart, and recent update
Offers a workaround that meets the 30-minute deadline
Explains each step in plain language without jargon
Logs the ticket and follows up to confirm the fix
q: I have a client call in half an hour. Can't you just fix this right now?
I already restarted it. Do I really have to do that again?
So what do I do if this happens again tomorrow?

c: Brightwater Elementary School, a school with 40 teachers
s: Mr. Brooks's classroom computer takes over five minutes to start, freezes when he opens the grade book, and recently displayed a message that the disk is almost full. He has a class set of tests to enter and a parent meeting this afternoon. The computer is four years old and has a 256 GB drive.

You can check the system, free up disk space, remove unneeded programs, and run updates. If hardware is failing, you may need to replace the drive or the machine. A replacement computer will take a week to arrive and costs $780; a new 512 GB drive costs $85 and takes about an hour to install.
The judge will play Mr. Brooks. You have 7 minutes to troubleshoot, explain your findings and recommend a solution.
f: Computer age: 4 years; drive: 256 GB, 98% full
Startup time: over 5 minutes; the grade book freezes
Possible causes: full disk, too many startup programs, failing drive or low memory
Options: clean up and update now; replace the drive ($85, 1 hour); replace the computer ($780, one week)
Mr. Brooks has a parent meeting at 3 p.m. today
n: Uses a systematic process: gather symptoms, check the simple causes first, test and document
Checks disk usage, startup programs and drive health
Explains that a full disk slows the computer and that a backup should come before any work
Compares cleanup, a new drive and a new computer with pros and cons
Recommends a solution that fits his schedule, such as cleanup today and a drive upgrade this week
Explains the steps in plain language and logs the ticket
q: Will I lose my grade book if you change the drive?
Why does a full drive make it so slow?
Can I have my computer ready for the meeting at 3?

c: Riverbend Dental Group, a practice with 20 employees and a growing number of devices
s: Riverbend Dental Group has had several IT problems: employees use personal passwords that rarely change, software updates are skipped, two laptops were lost last year, and nobody knows how many computers the practice owns. The practice owner wants to organize IT management and has a budget of $9,000 for the year.

The practice owner (judge) wants you to recommend policies and tools for asset tracking, security, user accounts, backups and software updates. The options are to hire a managed service provider, purchase management software and handle it in-house, or create basic written policies with training.
You have 7 minutes to present your analysis and recommend a plan.
f: Devices: about 32 computers, tablets and printers (not formally tracked)
Lost laptops last year: 2, with no encryption
Managed service provider: about $650 a month
Management software: $2,400 a year plus about 5 hours a month of staff time
Policy and training approach: about $1,000 for templates and a half-day session
n: Identifies IT management needs: inventory, accounts, updates, backups and security
Compares a managed provider, software and policies, with costs and pros and cons
Recommends a plan that fits $9,000, possibly combining software and policies
Proposes password rules, multi-factor authentication and device encryption
Includes an asset inventory and a lifecycle plan for replacing old equipment
Creates a support process, such as a ticket system and response targets
q: What is the single biggest risk in our current setup?
Why do we need to track every device?
How would you get the staff to follow new rules?

c: Maple Street Bakery, a bakery with a new online ordering system
j: the owner, Mrs. Kim, who is not comfortable with technology
s: Mrs. Kim opened an online ordering page last month and is not sure how it works. Customers have ordered but she is missing notification emails, can't find some orders, and doesn't understand the difference between the website, the payment system and her email. She is worried she will lose orders during the holiday season.

You are the help desk associate. Your job is to explain, in plain language, how the pieces of the system work together, help her find the missing orders, and show her what to do when something goes wrong. You must avoid jargon and make her feel comfortable.
The judge will play Mrs. Kim. You have 7 minutes to teach and solve the problem.
f: Online ordering page: hosted by a web service; payments handled by a separate payment processor
Notification emails: going to an old email address Mrs. Kim rarely checks
Missing orders: 4 orders appear in the payment processor but not in her order list
Holiday season starts in 10 days
Available fixes: change the notification email, show her where orders appear, set up a checklist
m: a call and screen-share with the owner
d: explain the system and resolve the issues
n: Explains the pieces using everyday comparisons, such as a storefront, a cash register and a mailbox
Finds the cause by checking the notification email address
Walks her through locating and confirming the four missing orders
Shows how to check orders daily and where to get help
Offers a simple checklist for the holiday rush
Shows patience and confirms understanding at each step
q: I don't understand why I need three different logins for all of this.
What if I miss an order and a customer is angry?
Can you write down the steps for me?

c: Northwind Marketing, an agency of 60 employees with a busy IT help desk
s: The IT service desk at Northwind Marketing receives about 90 tickets a week, but the average response time is 9 hours, and a recent survey shows that employees rate IT support 2.9 out of 5. Tickets are emailed to a shared inbox, there is no priority system, and two technicians cover all issues.

The operations director (judge) wants to improve service without hiring another full-time person. Options include a ticketing system with priorities, an employee self-service knowledge base, a contracted after-hours service, or reassigning one marketing coordinator to part-time IT support.
You have 7 minutes to explain the problems, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and recommend a plan.
f: Tickets: about 90 a week; average first response 9 hours
Employee satisfaction with IT: 2.9 out of 5
Ticketing system: about $1,500 a year; knowledge base: $900 a year plus 20 hours of writing
After-hours service: $400 a month
Common tickets: password resets (30%), printer problems (15%), software access (20%)
d: present your service desk improvement plan
n: Uses ticket data to find the biggest problems (30% password resets)
Describes service levels, prioritization and escalation
Compares ticketing, self-service and extra staffing with costs and pros and cons
Recommends a combination, such as a ticketing system plus self-service password reset
Sets targets, such as first response under 2 hours for high priority
Measures success with response time, resolution time and satisfaction
q: Why do password resets matter so much?
How would you decide which tickets come first?
What would you tell employees who are used to emailing their favorite technician?
